title: Sisters in Science
abstract: Author Diann Jordan took a journey to find out what inspired and daunted black women in their desire to become scientists in America. Letting 18 prominent black women scientists talk for themselves, Sisters in Science becomes an oral history stretching across decades and disciplines and desires. From Yvonne Clark, the first black woman to be awarded a B.S. in mechanical engineering to Georgia Dunston, a microbiologist who is researching the genetic code for her race, to Shirley Jackson, whose aspiration led to the presidency of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Jordan has created a significant record of women who persevered to become firsts in many of their fields. It all began for Jordan when she was asked to give a presentation on black women scientists. She found little information and little help. After almost nine years of work, the stories of black women scientists can finally be told.

Short impact summary

Sisters in Science (2006), published by Purdue University, has no recorded citations yet, but it has been downloaded 416 times. Beyond that, it is used in teaching.

Full narrative

Sisters in Science by Diann Jordan was published by Purdue University in 2006. Conceptually, the work connects to Presentation (obstetrics), Presidency, Race (biology), Oral history and Gender studies.

OpenAlex records no citations for the book so far.

In teaching, it is discussed in 1 recorded lecture. It has been downloaded 416 times via OAPEN. It is recorded in 5 library collections. Its subject matter aligns with Gender equality among the Sustainable Development Goals.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Sisters in Science shows clear early scholarly and educational reach rather than citation-based uptake: it has 416 OAPEN downloads, appears in teaching-related contexts including one YouTube discussion, and is held by libraries with subject coverage centered on women scientists and African American women scientists. The book also aligns with the gender equality SDG, reinforcing its relevance for gender-and-science scholarship and pedagogy.

Full narrative

Diann Jordan’s Sisters in Science is an oral-history-driven scholarly book that documents the experiences of Black women scientists across disciplines and generations. Its strongest record of influence is educational and library-based: the book is openly available through OAPEN, has accumulated 416 downloads, and is represented in library collections under subjects such as women scientists, African American scientists, African American women scientists, biography, and Black scientists. Together, these signals suggest that the book is being used as a reference point for learning, discovery, and context-setting in classrooms and collections.

The teaching signal is especially notable. The book is discussed in a recorded YouTube interview with the author, indicating that it has found a place in public-facing educational conversation. That kind of attention points to pedagogical value and accessibility, even though the broader record remains sparse on formal adoption indicators. The available evidence supports the interpretation that the book functions as a pedagogical anchor for discussions of race, gender, and scientific careers.

In terms of scholarly visibility, the citation record is still minimal in the sources provided: OpenAlex reports 0 citations, and the book has 1 scite mention. This does not diminish the book’s significance, but it does indicate that its influence is being expressed more through access, teaching, and collection presence than through citation accumulation at this stage. The record is therefore best read as a book with visible circulation and clear thematic importance, rather than as one with a developed citation footprint.

The book’s subject profile and SDG alignment sharpen that interpretation. Its concepts connect it to oral history, gender studies, sociology, history, and race, while the SDG match for gender equality suggests policy and social relevance beyond the academy. In combination, these signals show a work positioned at the intersection of scholarship, representation, and education, with the clearest impact in how it supports conversations about Black women in science and the structures that shape scientific participation.
